result: Genomic profiling of 30 lymphatic malformations revealed uniformly low tumor mutational burden with PIK3CA mutations (n=20, 67%) and NRAS mutations (n=5, 17%) as the most common alterations, which were mutually exclusive. The mutations had low variant allele frequencies (median 6%, range 1-38%) consistent with low tumor purity.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5, C32-C36, C39-C40 provide converging evidence from NGS profiling of the cohort. The mutational burden data (C32-C33), mutation frequencies (C3-C4, C34), mutual exclusivity (C5), and VAF analysis (C39-C40) are all directly derived from the genomic profiling and are internally consistent. The low VAF is appropriately interpreted in the context of low tumor purity (C31, C40).

result: All four lymphatic malformations with kaposiform histology (13% of cohort) harbored NRAS mutations, showing significant enrichment of NRAS mutations (p=0.00018) and absence of PIK3CA mutations (p=0.0046) in this histologic subtype compared to conventional LMs.
evaluation: Claims C6, C30, C41-C46 provide strong evidence for the histology-genotype correlation. The histopathological classification (C30, C41-C42) was performed by expert review, and the statistical analysis (C45-C46) demonstrates significant association. The 4/4 NRAS mutations in kaposiform cases (C44) with appropriate statistical testing supports this finding, though the small sample size (n=4) is a limitation.

result: One PIK3CA/NRAS wild-type lymphatic malformation harbored a GOPC-ROS1 fusion with a ROS1 missense mutation, a fusion type previously reported in pediatric gliomas and adult lung cancers that may be sensitive to ROS1 inhibitors.
evaluation: Claims C37-C38, C86 describe a rare genomic alteration identified in one case. The fusion was detected by NGS (C37) and is supported by citations to prior literature documenting similar fusions in other tumor types (C38, C86). While based on a single case, the finding is well-documented and appropriately contextualized.

result: The index patient (Patient #9) was a 23-year-old male who presented with abdominal pain and was found to have a large retroperitoneal/pancreatic lymphatic malformation harboring a PIK3CA H1047R mutation with confirmed PI3Kα pathway activation by immunohistochemistry.
evaluation: Claims C47-C53 provide comprehensive clinical, radiologic, pathologic, and molecular characterization of the index patient. The clinical presentation (C47-C49), histopathology (C50), genomic findings (C51-C52), and IHC confirmation of pathway activation (C53) are all directly documented with supporting figures. The characterization is thorough and well-supported.

result: The index patient achieved a rapid and durable complete radiologic response to alpelisib (350 mg daily) within 1 year, maintained for 2 years without adverse events. After discontinuation, the lesion recurred within weeks but responded again to re-treatment, with ongoing partial response for over 3 years.
evaluation: Claims C7, C58-C67 document the clinical trial outcomes with serial imaging and clinical assessments. The rapid response (C59, C62), complete response at 1 year (C63), lack of toxicity (C60), recurrence after discontinuation (C66), and response to re-treatment (C67) are all documented with radiologic evidence (Figure 2). The N-of-1 trial design and longitudinal follow-up provide strong evidence for drug efficacy in this specific case.

result: LM-derived lymphatic endothelial cells harboring a PIK3CA H1047L mutation (same locus as the index patient) demonstrated concentration-dependent sensitivity to alpelisib in vitro with an IC50 of 4.72×10⁻⁹ M at 24 hours.
evaluation: Claims C68-C71 provide in vitro validation of alpelisib sensitivity. The cell line characterization (C68-C69), dose-response curve (C70), and IC50 determination (C71) are documented with experimental data (Figure 3). The experiments provide mechanistic support for the clinical response, though the cell line is from a different patient with a similar mutation (H1047L vs H1047R).

result: The index patient had a reduced ejection fraction (47%) on screening echocardiogram that normalized after 2 months of alpelisib treatment, which was hypothesized to be artefactual due to circulatory volume sequestration in the large abdominal mass.
evaluation: Claims C54-C57, C61 describe cardiac findings and their interpretation. While the EF measurements are documented (C54-C55) and normalization after treatment is observed (C61), the hypothesis that the initial low EF was artefactual (C57) is speculative and not definitively proven. The patient's lack of cardiac symptoms (C56) supports the hypothesis, but alternative explanations (e.g., true cardiac dysfunction that improved with treatment) cannot be excluded.

result: Whole-genome sequencing of the index patient confirmed the PIK3CA H1047R mutation (VAF 11%) and identified few other somatic coding mutations. A PIK3C2B variant (R458Q) detected by the clinical panel was confirmed to be germline.
evaluation: Claims C72-C73, C116 describe WGS findings that extend beyond the clinical panel. The confirmation of the PIK3CA mutation (C72), paucity of other mutations (C73), and germline status of the PIK3C2B variant (C116) are all directly derived from WGS data. The findings are consistent with the low mutational burden observed in the cohort.

result: RNA-seq analysis of the index patient's lymphatic malformation identified 668 upregulated and 850 downregulated genes compared to normal controls, with enrichment of genes involved in vascular development, cell motility, and inflammatory response. Several highly induced genes (CHI3L1, GPX1, PLIN1, PLIN4, JAK3) have been linked to growth/survival in other tumor types.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 describe RNA-seq findings with differential expression analysis and GO enrichment. The gene counts (C74), functional associations (C75-C76), and JAK3 expression (C77) are derived from transcriptomic data with appropriate statistical thresholds. However, the choice of normal tissue controls (bladder, colon, kidney, salivary gland) is questionable as acknowledged in C119, which may affect interpretation.

result: The lymphatic malformation cohort was predominantly pediatric (median age 9 years, range 1-45) with slight female predominance (57%). Seven patients (23%) had overgrowth syndromes, 12 (40%) had multifocal disease, and histopathologic purity ranged from 10-70% (median 20%).
evaluation: Claims C24-C29, C31 provide demographic and clinical characteristics of the cohort derived from clinical records and pathologic review. These descriptive statistics are straightforward and well-documented in Table 1. The data provide important context for interpreting the genomic findings.

result: Three of five patients (60%) with NRAS-mutant lymphatic malformations had failed prior sirolimus treatment. Reports suggest some NRAS-mutant LMs may respond to MEK inhibitors.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 document treatment history and cite literature on potential therapeutic options. The sirolimus failure rate (C84) is derived from cohort data, and the MEK inhibitor potential (C85) is supported by citation to prior literature (Dummer et al., 2017). This provides important clinical context for NRAS-mutant cases.

result: The index patient did not experience hyperglycemia from alpelisib, consistent with reports of low hyperglycemia incidence in pediatric PROS patients. This suggests alpelisib-induced hyperglycemia may be less concerning in younger patients with more robust glucose homeostasis.
evaluation: Claims C95-C97 document the absence of hyperglycemia in the index patient (C95) and contextualize this with prior literature (C96). The speculation about age-related differences (C97) is reasonable but not definitively proven. The safety observation is important for clinical translation.

result: The recurrence of the lymphatic malformation after alpelisib discontinuation suggests that PI3Kα inhibitors do not completely eradicate LM-initiating cells and may need to be given long-term for sustained control.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are reasonable inferences based on the clinical observation of recurrence after treatment discontinuation (C66) and response to re-treatment (C67). However, this is based on a single case, and alternative explanations (e.g., incomplete initial response, new lesion development) cannot be excluded. The conclusion about long-term treatment need is appropriately cautious.

result: The majority of lymphatic malformations have potentially actionable driver mutations, with PIK3CA mutations dominating conventional histology cases and NRAS mutations enriched in kaposiform cases.
evaluation: Claims C87-C89, C124-C126 summarize the major findings of the genomic profiling study. The conclusion that most LMs have actionable mutations is supported by the data showing 25/30 (83%) cases with PIK3CA, NRAS, or GOPC-ROS1 alterations. The histology-genotype correlations are well-established by the data. This represents the primary conclusion of the study.

result: Wild-type PIK3CA/NRAS lymphatic malformations may harbor alterations in other pathway members not profiled by targeted sequencing. Comprehensive NGS or liquid biopsy approaches may be needed to identify actionable mutations in these cases.
evaluation: Claims C90-C92 are speculative recommendations for future work. While reasonable hypotheses, they are not supported by data from this study. The suggestion of liquid biopsy (C92) is particularly speculative given the lack of evidence that LMs shed detectable ctDNA. These represent knowledge gaps rather than supported findings.

result: The high frequency of PIK3CA mutations and the dramatic response in the index case suggest alpelisib may be highly effective for systemic treatment of PIK3CA-mutant lymphatic malformations, potentially as neoadjuvant therapy or primary treatment. Alpelisib may be more effective than mTOR inhibitors based on direct on-target activity and tolerability.
evaluation: Claims C93-C94, C100, C112 extrapolate from a single case to broader clinical implications. While the index case provides proof-of-concept (C7, C58-C67), the generalizability to other PIK3CA-mutant LMs is uncertain without additional cases. The comparison to mTOR inhibitors (C112) is based on indirect evidence. These are reasonable hypotheses requiring validation in larger studies.

result: Acquired resistance mechanisms to PI3Kα inhibitors involving RAS or PTEN mutations have been reported in other contexts and may arise in lymphatic malformation patients with longer follow-up.
evaluation: Claims C101-C102 cite established resistance mechanisms from cancer literature (Janku et al., 2014; Juric et al., 2017) and appropriately note these may occur in LM patients. This is reasonable speculation based on prior knowledge, though no resistance was observed in the index case during the follow-up period.

result: Prior studies by Luks et al. identified PIK3CA mutations in 94% of sporadic LMs and 90-94% of syndromic LMs. Venot et al. reported clinical responses to alpelisib in all 19 pediatric PROS patients, including those who failed mTOR inhibitors. mTOR inhibitors show ~50-60% response rates in unselected LMs.
evaluation: Claims C103-C111 accurately cite prior literature to contextualize the current findings. These citations are appropriately used to support the rationale for the study and interpret the results. The prior studies are correctly referenced and their findings accurately represented.

result: The low variant allele frequencies in lymphatic malformation tissue likely reflect low tumor cellularity, with most tissue composed of reactive stroma. PI3Kα pathway activation was most intense in lymphatic channel-lining endothelial cells, and gene expression patterns suggest an intense reactive response to clonal LM-LECs.
evaluation: Claims C117-C119 provide a mechanistic interpretation of the genomic and expression data. The inference about tumor cellularity (C117) is reasonable given the VAF and histopathologic purity data. The IHC localization (C118) directly supports the cellular origin. The gene expression interpretation (C119) is consistent with the data, though the authors appropriately note uncertainty about appropriate control tissues.

result: Studies are needed to determine if NRAS-mutant kaposiform LMs respond to MEK inhibitors. Wild-type cases may require comprehensive genomic analysis to identify actionable alterations. Systemic targeted therapy may be an option for patients not controlled by conventional treatments.
evaluation: Claims C127-C130 provide appropriate recommendations for future research and clinical practice based on the study findings. These are reasonable conclusions that follow logically from the data, though they represent future directions rather than established findings from this study.
